questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the elements of the imminence test
questions.stem: Table 1 reviews community bulletin notices that a city received last quarter. Which combination of findings must exist before any of these notices may be punished as incitement?

options.text: Intent to encourage imminent lawless action, together with a likelihood that the action will occur
A clear expression of anger at a law, published where the affected group could read it
options.misconception: treats published anger about law as punishable incitement

options.text: A written statement of intent, even if no unlawful action was foreseeable
options.misconception: believes a written intent alone satisfies the imminence test

options.text: An audience present at the reading, regardless of what followed the reading
options.misconception: assumes an audience alone completes the legal inquiry

questions.explanation: Incitement needs intent to stir imminent unlawful conduct and a real likelihood the conduct follows. Hostile opinion or an audience alone shows neither element, so the other readings fail.
questions.hint: Ask whether unlawful action is intended and likely to follow.

options.text: Most comments in the table are false threats, which suggests the newspaper attracts violent readers
options.misconception: treats total comment volume as a count of threats

options.text: Only comments about named people can ever be regulated under the First Amendment
options.misconception: believes naming someone is the only test for a threat

options.text: The four true-threat comments targeted a specific person, so they fall outside the First Amendment guarantee
The table shows that the advice column should be closed because threats appear at all
options.misconception: infers a content ban from the mere presence of threats

questions.explanation: True threats are statements conveying serious menace to a targeted person and receive no First Amendment protection. The four entries in the table meet that description, unlike ordinary opinion in the rest.
questions.hint: Focus on whether a statement conveys menace to a target.

questions.topic: The obscenity test and its elements
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the elements of the obscenity test
questions.stem: Table 3 lays out a four-box flow for the obscenity test: prurient interest, patent offensiveness, absence of serious merit, and the reaction of a reasonable person. Which box supplies the final step in the flow?

options.text: The box asking whether the work appeals to the prurient interest of a reasonable person
options.misconception: places the prurient-interest box at the end of the sequence

options.text: The box asking whether an ordinary reasonable person would find the work offensive
The box asking whether the work is patently offensive under community standards
options.misconception: assumes patent offensiveness is the final and decisive box

options.text: The box asking whether the work lacks serious literary, artistic, or political value
options.misconception: treats the serious-merit box as the last step required

questions.explanation: The obscenity test is conjunctive and ends by asking how a reasonable person would react. No single earlier box decides the question, so a flow ending at any of them is incomplete.
questions.hint: Ask which box a reasonable person answers at the end.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the validity of time, place, and manner rules
questions.stem: Table 4 lists three rules a council proposed for rallies outside a courthouse. Explain how time, place, and manner rules can bar speech without creating an unconstitutional restriction on content.

answer.exemplar: A valid time, place, and manner rule must be content neutral, leave open ample alternative channels of communication, and apply to all speakers alike. It may regulate the volume, duration, or location of a rally but cannot permit some messages and forbid others for the sake of their meaning.

questions.explanation: They are upheld only when content neutral, tailored to a significant interest, and leaving alternatives open. A rule selecting which messages may be heard becomes a content restriction.
questions.hint: Focus on content neutrality and alternative channels.

options.misconception: assumes licensing opens a channel of communication

options.misconception: ignores the presumption against prior restraint

A permissible protective order because delay always protects reputations
options.misconception: believes any reputational concern justifies holding a story

options.misconception: assumes professional discretion immunizes publishing decisions

questions.learningObjective: Assess a statute for facial overbreadth

options.text: The statute is valid because the government may punish speech that tends to cause unrest
options.misconception: treats unrest as a sufficient ground to punish all advocacy

The work where two of the three boxes were answered yes

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Contrast content-based and content-neutral rules
questions.stem: Table 13 compares two parking lot rules: one bans all large signs, the other bans signs about a named candidate. Explain why the rules receive different First Amendment treatment.

answer.exemplar: The rule banning all large signs is content neutral, because it applies the same limit to every message and leaves open smaller signs and conversations. The rule aimed at signs about a named candidate selects speech by its subject, so it is content based and receives the strictest scrutiny the government can satisfy.

questions.explanation: A rule applying the same limit to every message is content neutral and gets ordinary review. A rule aimed at a named candidate message is content based and gets strict scrutiny.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule trigger is the message subject.

options.misconception: treats evidence of planning as proof of imminent action

questions.learningObjective: Explain the presumption against prior restraint
questions.stem: Table 31 records a hearing officer order that a weekly newspaper not publish a photograph pending review. Explain why such an order is likely to be unconstitutional.

answer.exemplar: An order forbidding publication is a prior restraint, and the law presumes such restraints to be unconstitutional because they chill expression before the public has ever seen it. The government bears an unusually heavy burden of proving the restraint is necessary, and a pending review of a photograph already obtained rarely meets that burden.

questions.explanation: Prior restraints carry a heavy presumption against constitutionality since they suppress speech before the public judges it. The government must show overriding need, and routine pending review is not enough.

answer.exemplar: A court asks whether the statute on its face reaches a substantial amount of constitutionally protected expression, such as political discussion or criticism of officials. questions.learningObjective: List the elements an incitement prosecution must prove
questions.stem: Table 49 records a case where a crowd assembled after a rumor circulated online, and no organizer was identified. Explain what the government would need to prove to convict under the incitement doctrine.

answer.exemplar: The government would have to show that a defendant intended to encourage imminent lawless action, that the defendant words were likely to produce that action, and that the action actually followed. questions.learningObjective: Explain how courts identify true threats
questions.stem: Table 58 lists statements a speaker made after a fight, with the audience reactions recorded. Explain how a court decides which of these statements qualify as true threats.

answer.exemplar: A court asks whether a reasonable person in the victim position would perceive a serious menace in the statement, judged in context and from the listener perspective rather than the speaker intent. Statements that merely frighten, offend, or predict unpleasant events do not qualify, while those directed at an identifiable person with menace do.

questions.explanation: The test is objective and contextual: a reasonable listener must perceive serious menace, and context such as prior violence can bear on that perception. Speaker intent is beside the point.
questions.hint: Use the listener perspective and the surrounding context.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The obscenity test and its elements
questions.learningObjective: Compute the number of works meeting every element
questions.stem: Table 59 lists 300 works reviewed under the obscenity test. Ninety failed the prurient interest element, sixty failed the patent offensiveness element, and twenty failed the serious merit element, each work counted under exactly one element. How many of the three hundred works satisfied every element of the test?
questions.explanation: The failures total 90 plus 60 plus 20, which is 170 works, and 300 minus 170 leaves 130 works meeting every element. Those are the works the statute elements would reach.
questions.hint: Subtract all failures from the total reviewed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Characterize a time, place, and manner rule

stimulus.body: Section 12. Sound amplification. No amplified sound may be used within 300 feet of a hospital between the hours of 8 p.m. and 7 a.m. This section applies to all persons equally and does not depend on the content of any message conveyed.

questions.stem: Table 60 places the excerpt beside the city enforcement log. Which description of Section 12 is most accurate?

options.text: A content based restriction because it restricts speech at particular times
options.misconception: confuses time restrictions with content restrictions

options.text: A prior restraint because it stops speakers before they can be heard
options.misconception: labels every restriction on amplification a prior restraint

options.text: An unconstitutional time, place, and manner rule because it applies to all speakers
options.misconception: believes evenhanded application makes a rule unconstitutional

options.text: A content neutral time and place rule subject to ordinary proportionality review

questions.explanation: The excerpt regulates sound, location, and hour rather than subject matter, and says so expressly. Such a rule is judged on fit and available alternatives, not on strict scrutiny.
questions.hint: Check whether the rule depends on the message.
